analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Conditions Survey, 36.8 percent of firms in finance and insurance reported using AI in the most recent measurement period, up from 35.5 percent in the prior period, making it one of the more consistently measured sectors in that dataset. The figures cover the broad finance and insurance category rather than banking alone, but they establish a clear upward trend in active use rather than mere experimentation.

Banking is unusual among industries in that AI governance predates the current AI boom by more than a decade. The Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 guidance, issued in 2011 and catalogued in its supervisory letters index, established model risk management requirements that credit scoring and anti-money-laundering models have operated under ever since. Any bank deploying a new AI model, whether a traditional statistical tool or a large language model, enters a regulatory environment that already has vocabulary, examination procedures, and board-level accountability expectations built around model validation and oversight.

The sourced points note that Treasury has framed the supervisory conversation at a higher level, mapping the uses, opportunities, and risks of AI in financial services in a dedicated report on the topic. That framing matters because it signals that regulators are treating generative AI and advanced automation as an extension of existing supervisory priorities rather than as something entirely novel requiring a fresh legal architecture.

On the competitive intelligence side, the Evident AI Banking Index is described as the closest thing banking has to a public AI scoreboard, scoring major global banks across dozens of quantitative maturity metrics spanning talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency. Its existence reflects an industry where relative AI capability is now treated as a material strategic differentiator worth measuring systematically across institutions.

For practitioners evaluating deployment, the practical takeaway from this body of material is that the compliance pathway is better marked in banking than in most sectors, but it is also more demanding. SR 11-7 requires documented validation, clear model inventories, and ongoing performance monitoring, which means the organizational investment required to deploy responsibly is front-loaded. The open financial models catalogued on this site, drawn from the Hugging Face Hub's most-downloaded finance-tuned models, illustrate that the supply of candidate models is large, but selecting and governing them within an SR 11-7 framework remains the determinative constraint on deployment speed.
